Movement Disorders 
Vol. 6, No. 1, 1991, pp. 12-20 
0 1991 Movement Disorder Society 
Stiff-Person Syndrome: An Autoimmune Disease 
Philip Blum and Joseph Jankovic 
Department of Neurology, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, Texas, U.S.A. 
Summary: Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is characterized by progressive, usu- 
ally symmetric rigidity of the axial muscles with superimposed painful spasms 
precipitated by tactile stimuli, passive stretch, volitional movement of affected 
or unaffected muscles, startling noises, and emotional stimuli. Electromyog- 
raphy demonstrates continuous normal motor unit potentials in the affected 
muscles. Both the rigidity and the spasms are relieved by sleep, general anes- 
thesia, myoneural blockade, peripheral nerve blockade, and partially by diaz- 
epam. Evidence for an autoimmune etiology of SPS includes its association 
with other autoimmune diseases and autoantibodies and the presence of anti- 
bodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) in the cerebrospinal fluid 
(CSF) of many affected patients. We describe two patients with this syndrome 
who had GAD antibodies in both CSF and serum. Partial relief of the symp- 
toms in these patients by corticosteroid therapy provides additional evidence 
of an autoimmune etiology of SPS and of the role of immunotherapy in its 
treatment. Key Words: Stiff-person syndrome-Autoimmune diseases-corti- 
costeroid drugs. 
Stiff-man syndrome was first described by 
Moersch and Woltman (1) in a series of 14 cases in 
1956. The world’s literature was critically reviewed 
and diagnostic criteria were proposed by Gordon et 
al. (2) in 1967. Because the disease affects both men 
and women, we prefer the term “stiff-person’’ syn- 
drome (SPS). Patients with SPS have progressive, 
usually symmetric.rigidity of the axial muscles, and 
painful spasms that may fluctuate in intensity. 
Spasms may be precipitated by tactile stimuli, pas- 
sive stretch, volitional movement of affected or un- 
affected muscles, startling noises, and emotional 
stimuli. There is often tenderness and palpable ri- 
gidity of the axial and proximal limb musculature. 
Deep tendon reflexes are occasionally increased, 
but may be decreased. Electromyography (EMG) 
demonstrates continuous normal motor unit poten-

tials in the affected muscles despite the patient’s 
attempts to relax. Both the rigidity and the spasms 
are at least partially relieved by sleep, general an- 
esthesia, myoneural blockade, peripheral nerve 
blockade, and usually, diazepam. The improvement 
in the cardinal symptoms is accompanied by cessa- 
tion of the continuous motor unit potentials. Cranial 
nerve involvement, respiratory compromise, and 
deforming skeletal sequelae 
are common. Myoclo- 
nus, seizures, and psychiatric illnesses have also 
been reported in some patients. 
Treatment of SPS has changed little since Howard 
(3) introduced diazepam as the drug of choice in 
1963. However, in 1988 Solimena et al. (4) provided 
the first solid evidence of an autoimmune mecha- 
nism of the disease and introduced hope for new 
effective therapies. These investigators demon- 
strated the presence of autoantibodies against glu- 
tamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) in both the serum 
and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of their patient

with the syndrome. In their follow-up report, Soli- 
mena et al. (5) observed GAD autoantibodies in 20

STIFF-PERSON SYNDROME 13 
of 33 patients with the syndrome. We describe here 
two patients with SPS found to have GAD autoanti- 
bodies in their sera and CSF, and whose associated 
autoimmune diseases, other autoantibodies, and re- 
sponse to corticosteroid drugs provide additional 
evidence of an autoimmune etiology and a role for 
immunotherapy in this disabling disease. 
PATIENT 1 
A 63-year-old Hispanic woman was referred for 
evaluation of increased tone in her lower extremi- 
ties. She had been well until 6 years previously, 
when she began to experience occasional episodes 
of sudden, painful stiffening of the left hip and knee, 
usually provoked by walking. The spasms lasted 
10-15 s, and then resolved spontaneously. Her 
symptoms progressed, increasing in severity and 
frequency, and in June 1988 the patient's left leg 
became persistently stiff, rendering her unable to 
walk. At that time, she also had severe, chronic, 
recurrent back and abdominal pain. By the end of 
the year, her right leg had also begun to stiffen. The 
stiffness was much decreased during sleep. There 
was no history of diabetes, trauma, seizures, myo- 
clonus, weakness, or sensory difficulties. Her or- 
thopedist had prescribed multiple medications 
including propoxyphene napsylate and acetamino- 
phen (Darvocet), quinine sulfate, phenytoin, so- 
dium dantrolene, carbamazepine, baclofen, and di- 
azepam. Only the last two provided at least partial 
relief of her spasms. Past medical history was sig- 
nificant only for a cholecystectomy in 1976 and 
treated pulmonary tuberculosis with documented 
recovery. She has not used alcohol or tobacco prod- 
ucts. No one else in her family has had symptoms 
similar to hers. Both of her sisters died of compli- 
cations of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus 
(IDDM). Review of systems was significant for 
long-standing vitiligo. 
Physical examination on admission to our service 
revealed a small, chronically ill-appearing woman 
lying in bed. She had vitiligo of the hands, feet, and 
neck. There was increased tone and tenderness in 
the muscles of the neck. Her paraspinous muscles 
were markedly rigid and tender and she had severe 
kyphoscoliosis. Tone and strength in the arms was 
normal. However, tone was markedly increased in 
her legs, with palpable rigidity and tenderness of the 
muscles. Her feet were held in the equinus position 
and her knees were hyperextended by her stiffness 
(videotape segment 1). There were no fascicula- 
tions. Strength could not be assessed because of the 
rigidity. Plantar response was silent, and deep ten- 
don reflexes could not be elicited in the knees or 
ankles. Functionally, the patient was unable to walk 
because of the stiffness in her legs and was unable 
to sit up because of the deformity of her spine. She 
had an intact intellect and sensorium and there were 
no other neurologic abnormalities. 
Results of routine laboratory studies including se- 
rum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), cre- 
atinine, glucose, and liver enzymes were normal; 
creatinine phosphokinase was 256. Lyme titers 
were negative. Radiographs of the chest and lum- 
bosacral spine demonstrated arthritic changes only. 
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy, ultrasound of the 
abdomen, and computed tomography (CT) of the 
abdomen all were normal. Lumbar myelogram, CT 
of the brain, and magnetic resonance (MR) imaging 
of the lumbosacral spine were also normal. Muscle

biopsy revealed mild neurogenic atrophy and type 
I1 atrophy. A complete myelogram revealed only 
mild cervical spondylosis with neither stenosis of 
the canal nor cord compression. Conduction studies 
of the right posterior tibial nerve were normal at 52 
m/s, whereas that of the left posterior tibial nerve 
was slightly slowed at 44 mls. EMG demonstrated 
continuous spontaneous motor unit activity in all 
tested muscles of the left leg and in the lumbar and 
thoracic paraspinous muscles up to the midthoracic 
level bilaterally. Intermittent, spontaneous motor 
unit activity also occurred in the right leg and could 
be provoked by startling or tactile stimulation. 
There were no fasciculations, fibrillations, or posi- 
tive sharp waves. 
Spinal epidural blockade was performed with tet- 
racaine (Pontocaine) at the T9 level. The patient's 
pain was relieved, and her rigidity decreased 
enough to allow 20" of active flexion in the left knee 
and 40" in the right (videotape segment 2). EMG 
recording demonstrated cessation of the continuous 
motor activity within 10 min. Routine studies of the 
CSF taken at the time of the myelogram including 
glucose, protein, and cell count were all normal and 
no oligoclonal bands were detected. GAD autoanti- 
bodies, assayed by Dr. Solimena and Dr. De Camilli 
(5), were present in both the serum and CSF by 
light-microscopy immunocytochemistry and West- 
ern blot. In addition, autoantibodies to islet cells 
and gastric parietal cells were present in the serum. 
This patient was reported as case 17 in the second 
report of Solimena et al. (5). 
The patient was unable to tolerate diazepam in 
high doses because of excessive sedation. The com-

bination of 50 mg of baclofen and 30 mg of diazepam 
daily provided only modest relief of symptoms. One 
hundred milligrams of prednisone per day was 
added to this regimen. Within 10 days, the patient 
noted a marked decrease in her stiffness and spasm. 
One year later, baclofen has been discontinued, di- 
azepam has been decreased to 15 mg per day, and 
prednisone is slowly being tapered down from 40 
mg every other day. The stiffness in her hips, 
knees, and back is markedly reduced. Residual 
stiffness holds her ankles in a position of plantar 
flexion bilaterally. She is now capable of sitting 
without aid, although she cannot walk because of 
her ankle contractures. 
PATIENT 2 
A 53-year-old black man was referred for evalu- 
ation of a 2?h-year history of progressive stiffness of 
the lower extremities. His initial symptom was in- 
voluntary upward curling of the toes of both feet. 
Stiffness subsequently developed in the remaining 
muscles of his legs. At the same time, he began to 
have chronic neck and low-back pain. One year be- 
fore admission, the patient also began to have pain- 
ful spasms of his legs superimposed on his stiffness, 
usually provoked by passive stretching. His wife 
noted that his spasms ceased and his stiffness re- 
solved somewhat during sleep. He began to require 
assistance arising from bed and walking. There was 
no history of diabetes, trauma, seizures, myoclo- 
nus, weakness, or sensory symptoms. The patient 
had been treated unsuccessfully with nonsteroidal 
antiinflammatory medications, sodium dantrolene, 
carbamazepine, trihexyphenidyl, and carbidopa/ 
levodopa (Sinemet). Treatment with phenytoin af- 
forded him mild relief. Low-dose diazepam moder- 
ately improved his stiffness and he was able to walk 
without assistance. One of the patient’s sisters has 
IDDM; otherwise, the family history was unre- 
markable. 
General physical and neurological examination 
results were normal except for the motor system. 
Tone and strength were normal in the arms, but 
tone was markedly increased in all muscle groups of 
the legs, with dystonic posturing of both feet man- 
ifesting as extension of the metatarsal-phalangeal 
joints and flexion of the distal interphalangeal 
joints. Strength of the legs was difficult to assess 
because of rigidity. Deep tendon reflexes were nor- 
mal throughout and plantar reflexes were silent. 
The patient walked stiffly and turned with great dif- 
ficulty. 
The following laboratory test results were nor- 
mal: electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, uric 
acid, calcium, phosphorus, total protein, albumin, 
serum electrophoresis, liver enzymes, folate, vita- 
min B 12, hemoglobin, hematocrit, mean corpuscular 
volume, platelet count, urinalysis, erythrocyte sed- 
imentation rate, rapid plasma reagin, antinuclear 
antibody, and rheumatoid factor. A 5-h glucose tol- 
erance test also showed normal results. A complete 
myelogram revealed mild lumbar and cervical 
spondylosis without stenosis of the canal. Radio- 
graphs of the chest and spine, electrocardiogram, 
electroencephalogram, and somatosensory evoked 
potentials were all unremarkable. Muscle biopsy 
was similar to that of patient 
1. MR imaging of the 
brain and spinal cord were normal. EMG revealed 
the presence of continuous spontaneous motor unit 
potentials in the muscles of the legs, which was 
abolished by spinal epidural block. As the block

began to wear off, the patient was able to move his 
legs nearly normally. CSF glucose, protein, and cell 
count were unremarkable and there were no oligo- 
clonal bands. CSF IgG/albumin ratio was normal. 
Autoantibodies to GAD were detected in both se- 
rum and CSF by the method of Solimena et al. (4). 
In addition, gastric parietal cell, pancreatic islet 
cell, microsomal, and thyroglobulin autoantibodies 
were all present in the patient’s serum. This patient 
was reported as case 20 in the second report of 
Solimena et al. (5). The human lymphocyte antigen 
(HLA) phenotype of the patient was A3,24; 
B14(w6),w57(w4); DRw6,7(DQw1 ,w3; DRw52,53). 
At the time of admission, diazepam therapy was 
withdrawn slowly to determine the baseline muscle 
stiffness of the patient. After a few days, he became 
markedly stiffer (videotape segment 1). The patient 
then began supplemental treatment with 100 mg of 
prednisone per day for 1 week and then 100 and 20 
mg on an alternate-day basis. Within 10 days of 
starting prednisone, the patient began to notice a 
marked decrease of his stiffness (videotape segment 
2). He was able to decrease the dose of diazepam 
from 40 to 20 mg per day. A year later, his dose of 
prednisone has been decreased to 40 mg every other 
day, but he still requires 20 mg of diazepam daily for 
residual stiffness. 
DISCUSSION 
Our two patients demonstrate the typical findings 
of SPS as described by Moersch and Woltman (1). 
Both fulfill the diagnostic criteria of Gordon et al. 
(2). In addition to spasm and progressive stiffness of

axial musculature, each patient had characteristic 
EMG findings of continuous motor unit activity. 
The stiffness as well as the EMG findings improved 
after spinal anesthesia. 
In addition, both of our patients exhibited evi- 
dence of autoimmunity. Patient l had vitiligo and 
two sisters with IDDM; patient 2 had no recognized 
clinical autoimmune diseases, but had several se- 
rum autoantibodies and a sister with IDDM. GAD

autoantibodies were present in the CSF and serum 
of both patients. The coexistence of other autoim- 
mune diseases and autoantibodies with SPS has 
been previously recognized by other investigators 
(Tables 1 and 2) (2,4,6-33).

the scarcity of autopsy material and the conflicting 
pathologic descriptions (15,25,34,35). The abolition 
of symptoms and of the characteristic EMG find- 
ings by peripheral nerve and motor endplate block- 
ing agents, sleep, and general and spinal anesthesia 
provide evidence for a CNS origin of the syndrome. 
Gordon et al. (2) suggested overactivity of the y 
motor neuron system or underactivity of their su- 
prasegmental inhibitory influences as the cause of 
the excessive discharges in the M motor neuron 
pool. Subsequent electrophysiologic and pharmaco- 
logic studies have provided evidence implicating 
dysfunction of GABAergic neurons in the y motor 
neuron system as the mechanism of the continuous 
muscle activity (13,17,26,36). Clinical improvement 
with diazepam, which is known to potentiate 
GABAergic transmission (13), also suggests in- 
volvement of the CNS in the pathophysiology of the 
syndrome. 
More recent investigation of the pathogenesis of

SPS has been directed toward understanding the 
cause of the presumed y motor system dysfunction. 
In their first report of a patient with SPS, epilepsy, 
type I diabetes, and elevated IgG/albumin ratio in 
the CSF, Solimena et al. (4) recovered antibody di- 
rected against GABAergic neurons. This antibody, 
recovered from the serum and CSF, demonstrated 
immunoreactivity by light-microscopy immunocy- 
tochemistry in 
a pattern identical to the cellular and 
subcellular distributions of GAD in rat and human 
brain and rat pancreatic islet cells. In addition, this 
antibody was found to recognize essentially one 
Movement Disorders, Vol. 6, No. I. 1991

18 P. BLUM AND J. JANKOVIC 
band comigrating with GAD on Western blot (4). In 
their subsequent study, they found these GAD au- 
toantibodies in 20 of 33 patients with SPS and again 
noted close association with a variety of other au- 
toimmune diseases, particularly IDDM (5). Because 
GAD is primarily an intracellular antigen, autoanti- 
bodies directed against this enzyme may represent a 
phenomenon secondary to the immunologic de- 
struction of GABAergic neurons. These observa- 
tions strongly support an autoimmune hypothesis 
for SPS. 
An autoimmune mechanism of disease was first 
proposed for SPS by Young (7) in 1966, because, in 
addition to motor complaints, his patient had per- 
nicious anemia and possible Hashimoto’s thyroid- 
itis. Autoimmune diseases often coexist in patients. 
For example, the occurrence of pernicious anemia 
is substantially increased in patients with idiopathic 
adrenal insufficiency, Grave’s disease, and vitiligo 
(37). Similarly, a striking number of autoimmune 
diseases occur in patients with SPS (Table 1). Of the 
84 patients who fulfill Gordon’s criteria (2) for SPS, 
15, or 18%, had clinical evidence of one or more 
autoimmune diseases. Three had pernicious ane- 
mia, four had vitiligo, and one patient developed 
myasthenia gravis after a spontaneous remission of 
stiff-person symptoms. Four of the 84 had hypothy- 
roidism and 2 had hyperthyroidism; both of these 
diseases may be autoimmune in origin. In addition, 
two patients were thought to have Hashimoto’s thy- 
roiditis. Our patient 1 had vitiligo as well as two 
sisters with IDDM. Patient 2 also had a sister with 
IDDM. Autoantibodies are also commonly found in 
the sera of patients with SPS (Table 2). In the sec- 
ond report of Solimena et al. (9, 19 of 20 patients 
with SPS and GAD autoantibody present in CSF or 
serum also had at least one other type of autoanti- 
body. Of those who did not have GAD antibody, 4 
of 12 had at least one other serum autoantibody 
present. Both patients described in this report had 
serum autoantibodies directed against islet cells and 
gastric parietal cells. Patient 2 also had microsomal 
and thyroglobulin antibodies. The remarkable num- 
ber of autoantibodies and autoimmune diseases in 
affected patients again suggests that SPS has an au- 
toimmune etiology. 
The relationship of SPS and diabetes mellitus de- 
serves special attention. The current hypothesis 
about the pathogenesis of IDDM is that an abnor- 
mal immune response to an unknown stimulus, pos- 
sibly a virus, is responsible for the development of 
IDDM in genetically predisposed individuals. 
Ninety-five percent of white patients with IDDM 
have HLA DR4 and/or DR3, suggesting that the 
disease is mediated by regulatory or structural vari- 
ation of HLA molecules (38). Review of the litera- 
ture reveals that 7 of the 84 (8%) patients were re- 
ported to have IDDM, a frequency more than 30 times 
that of the general population (0.25%) (39). Thirteen 
additional patients were reported to have DM but 
the type was not reported. Another two patients had 
islet cell antibodies (ICA) without clinical evidence 
of DM. In one study, patients with ICA who had 
relatives with IDDM had a 100% probability of de- 
veloping IDDM within 5 years (38). Thus, the cal- 
culated 30-fold increase in the frequency of IDDM 
in patients with SPS is a conservative estimate. 
The relationship between IDDM and SPS may 
not be coincidental. The peculiar configurations of

HLA-determined immunoregulatory molecules im- 
plicated in the pathogenesis of IDDM (39) may rep- 
resent the altered immune system via which autoim- 
munity to GABAergic cells in the CNS develops. 
The demonstration of HLA phenotypes common to 
both diseases supports this hypothesis. HLA DR3 
and DR4, the alleles most commonly associated 
with IDDM in whites, were present in all three pa- 
tients with SPS in whom this antigen was typed, 
including one who did not have IDDM (Table 2). In 
addition, four of five patients of Williams et al. (29) 
had HLA B44, which is in linkage dysequilibrium 
with DR4 (40). Typing of HLA-DR was not done in 
these patients. Our patient 2 had neither HLA DR3 
nor DR4. However, this patient is black and the 
HLA phenotypes responsible for susceptibility to 
IDDM in populations other than whites are not well 
established (38). Nevertheless, specific HLA types 
may represent the etiologic link between IDDM and 
SPS . 
Improvement of SPS symptoms with immuno- 
therapy provides additional strong support for the 
autoimmune hypothesis of the disease as well as 
hope for curative treatment. Plasmapheresis has 
had a variable effect. Vicari et al. (28) reported 
striking improvement in their patient after 10 days 
of every-other-day plasma exchange. Harding et al. 
(30) reported one patient who had no improvement 
after 5 days of plasma exchange and another who 
failed to improve after combined treatment with 
plasmapheresis, azathioprine, and prednisone. She 
and her colleagues point out, however, that because 
GAD autoantibody synthesis seems to occur in- 
trathecally, exchange of plasma would theoretically 
not be expected to benefit these patients. 
Movement Disorders, Vol. 6, No. I, 1991

STIFF-PERSON SYNDROME 19 
Corticosteroid immunotherapy has been more 
successful. Piccolo (28) has reported two cases in 
which patients responded dramatically within 10 
days of steroid treatment. One patient treated with 
prednisone 100 mg/day achieved a complete remis- 
sion. The second also responded to prednisone 100 
mg/day, but has had some residual contractures of 
affected muscles. Our two patients similarly had 
markedly reduced stiffness with improvement in 
their functioning and substantial reductions in their 
diazepam requirements. Residual contractures re- 
sulting from the prolonged muscle rigidity remain, 
however, and impair the function of both of our 
patients. Early intervention might be expected to 
produce more complete relief. 
In summary, two new cases of SPS are presented 
and the features of the disease are documented by 
videotape. Furthermore, we documented a marked 
decrease in stiffness and spasms in both patients 
after administration of corticosteroid drugs. They 
represent two of only four similarly treated patients 
with functional improvement after steroid therapy. 
The effectiveness of immunotherapy in these pa- 
tients adds to a growing body of evidence to support 
an autoimmune etiology of SPS.

reduced stiffness.

PATIENT 1 
A 63-year-old Hispanic woman was referred for 
evaluation of increased tone in her lower extremi- 
ties. She had been well until 6 years previously, 
when she began to experience occasional episodes 
of sudden, painful stiffening of the left hip and knee, 
usually provoked by walking. The spasms lasted 
10-15 s, and then resolved spontaneously. Her 
symptoms progressed, increasing in severity and 
frequency, and in June 1988 the patient's left leg 
became persistently stiff, rendering her unable to 
walk. At that time, she also had severe, chronic, 
recurrent back and abdominal pain. By the end of 
the year, her right leg had also begun to stiffen. The 
stiffness was much decreased during sleep. There 
was no history of diabetes, trauma, seizures, myo- 
clonus, weakness, or sensory difficulties. Her or- 
thopedist had prescribed multiple medications 
including propoxyphene napsylate and acetamino- 
phen (Darvocet), quinine sulfate, phenytoin, so- 
dium dantrolene, carbamazepine, baclofen, and di- 
azepam. Only the last two provided at least partial 
relief of her spasms. Past medical history was sig- 
nificant only for a cholecystectomy in 1976 and 
treated pulmonary tuberculosis with documented 
recovery. She has not used alcohol or tobacco prod- 
ucts. No one else in her family has had symptoms 
similar to hers. Both of her sisters died of compli- 
cations of insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus 
(IDDM). Review of systems was significant for 
long-standing vitiligo. 
Physical examination on admission to our service 
revealed a small, chronically ill-appearing woman 
lying in bed. She had vitiligo of the hands, feet, and 
neck. There was increased tone and tenderness in 
the muscles of the neck. Her paraspinous muscles 
were markedly rigid and tender and she had severe 
kyphoscoliosis. Tone and strength in the arms was 
normal. However, tone was markedly increased in 
her legs, with palpable rigidity and tenderness of the 
muscles. Her feet were held in the equinus position 
and her knees were hyperextended by her stiffness 
(videotape segment 1). There were no fascicula- 
tions. Strength could not be assessed because of the 
rigidity. Plantar response was silent, and deep ten- 
don reflexes could not be elicited in the knees or 
ankles. Functionally, the patient was unable to walk 
because of the stiffness in her legs and was unable 
to sit up because of the deformity of her spine. She 
had an intact intellect and sensorium and there were 
no other neurologic abnormalities. 
Results of routine laboratory studies including se- 
rum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), cre- 
atinine, glucose, and liver enzymes were normal; 
creatinine phosphokinase was 256. Lyme titers 
were negative. Radiographs of the chest and lum- 
bosacral spine demonstrated arthritic changes only. 
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy, ultrasound of the 
abdomen, and computed tomography (CT) of the 
abdomen all were normal. Lumbar myelogram, CT 
of the brain, and magnetic resonance (MR) imaging 
of the lumbosacral spine were also normal.
segments.evidence: Patient 1 history, examination, investigations, and initial SPS features are described under the paper's Patient 1 heading.

segments.text:
biopsy revealed mild neurogenic atrophy and type 
I1 atrophy. A complete myelogram revealed only 
mild cervical spondylosis with neither stenosis of 
the canal nor cord compression. Conduction studies 
of the right posterior tibial nerve were normal at 52 
m/s, whereas that of the left posterior tibial nerve 
was slightly slowed at 44 mls. EMG demonstrated 
continuous spontaneous motor unit activity in all 
tested muscles of the left leg and in the lumbar and 
thoracic paraspinous muscles up to the midthoracic 
level bilaterally. Intermittent, spontaneous motor 
unit activity also occurred in the right leg and could 
be provoked by startling or tactile stimulation. 
There were no fasciculations, fibrillations, or posi- 
tive sharp waves. 
Spinal epidural blockade was performed with tet- 
racaine (Pontocaine) at the T9 level. The patient's 
pain was relieved, and her rigidity decreased 
enough to allow 20" of active flexion in the left knee 
and 40" in the right (videotape segment 2). EMG 
recording demonstrated cessation of the continuous 
motor activity within 10 min. Routine studies of the 
CSF taken at the time of the myelogram including 
glucose, protein, and cell count were all normal and 
no oligoclonal bands were detected. GAD autoanti- 
bodies, assayed by Dr. Solimena and Dr. De Camilli 
(5), were present in both the serum and CSF by 
light-microscopy immunocytochemistry and West- 
ern blot. In addition, autoantibodies to islet cells 
and gastric parietal cells were present in the serum. 
This patient was reported as case 17 in the second 
report of Solimena et al. (5).
segments.evidence: Patient 1 electrophysiology, response to spinal block, CSF/serum GAD antibodies, and other serum autoantibodies are reported.

daily provided only modest relief of symptoms. One 
hundred milligrams of prednisone per day was 
added to this regimen. Within 10 days, the patient 
noted a marked decrease in her stiffness and spasm. 
One year later, baclofen has been discontinued, di- 
azepam has been decreased to 15 mg per day, and 
prednisone is slowly being tapered down from 40 
mg every other day. The stiffness in her hips, 
knees, and back is markedly reduced. Residual 
stiffness holds her ankles in a position of plantar 
flexion bilaterally. She is now capable of sitting 
without aid, although she cannot walk because of 
her ankle contractures.
segments.evidence: Patient 1 treatment response to baclofen/diazepam and prednisone is described.

segments.text:
PATIENT 2 
A 53-year-old black man was referred for evalu- 
ation of a 2?h-year history of progressive stiffness of 
the lower extremities. His initial symptom was in- 
voluntary upward curling of the toes of both feet. 
Stiffness subsequently developed in the remaining 
muscles of his legs. At the same time, he began to 
have chronic neck and low-back pain. One year be- 
fore admission, the patient also began to have pain- 
ful spasms of his legs superimposed on his stiffness, 
usually provoked by passive stretching. His wife 
noted that his spasms ceased and his stiffness re- 
solved somewhat during sleep. He began to require 
assistance arising from bed and walking. There was 
no history of diabetes, trauma, seizures, myoclo- 
nus, weakness, or sensory symptoms. The patient 
had been treated unsuccessfully with nonsteroidal 
antiinflammatory medications, sodium dantrolene, 
carbamazepine, trihexyphenidyl, and carbidopa/ 
levodopa (Sinemet). Treatment with phenytoin af- 
forded him mild relief. Low-dose diazepam moder- 
ately improved his stiffness and he was able to walk 
without assistance. One of the patient’s sisters has 
IDDM; otherwise, the family history was unre- 
markable. 
General physical and neurological examination 
results were normal except for the motor system. 
Tone and strength were normal in the arms, but 
tone was markedly increased in all muscle groups of 
the legs, with dystonic posturing of both feet man- 
ifesting as extension of the metatarsal-phalangeal 
joints and flexion of the distal interphalangeal 
joints. Strength of the legs was difficult to assess 
because of rigidity. Deep tendon reflexes were nor- 
mal throughout and plantar reflexes were silent. 
The patient walked stiffly and turned with great dif- 
ficulty. 
The following laboratory test results were nor- 
mal: electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, uric 
acid, calcium, phosphorus, total protein, albumin, 
serum electrophoresis, liver enzymes, folate, vita- 
min B 12, hemoglobin, hematocrit, mean corpuscular 
volume, platelet count, urinalysis, erythrocyte sed- 
imentation rate, rapid plasma reagin, antinuclear 
antibody, and rheumatoid factor. A 5-h glucose tol- 
erance test also showed normal results. A complete 
myelogram revealed mild lumbar and cervical 
spondylosis without stenosis of the canal. Radio- 
graphs of the chest and spine, electrocardiogram, 
electroencephalogram, and somatosensory evoked 
potentials were all unremarkable. Muscle biopsy 
was similar to that of patient 
1. MR imaging of the 
brain and spinal cord were normal. EMG revealed 
the presence of continuous spontaneous motor unit 
potentials in the muscles of the legs, which was 
abolished by spinal epidural block.
segments.evidence: Patient 2 history, examination, routine studies, EMG findings, and response to epidural block are reported under the Patient 2 heading.

legs nearly normally. CSF glucose, protein, and cell 
count were unremarkable and there were no oligo- 
clonal bands. CSF IgG/albumin ratio was normal. 
Autoantibodies to GAD were detected in both se- 
rum and CSF by the method of Solimena et al. (4). 
In addition, gastric parietal cell, pancreatic islet 
cell, microsomal, and thyroglobulin autoantibodies 
were all present in the patient’s serum. This patient 
was reported as case 20 in the second report of 
Solimena et al. (5). The human lymphocyte antigen 
(HLA) phenotype of the patient was A3,24; 
B14(w6),w57(w4); DRw6,7(DQw1 ,w3; DRw52,53). 
At the time of admission, diazepam therapy was 
withdrawn slowly to determine the baseline muscle 
stiffness of the patient. After a few days, he became 
markedly stiffer (videotape segment 1). The patient 
then began supplemental treatment with 100 mg of 
prednisone per day for 1 week and then 100 and 20 
mg on an alternate-day basis. Within 10 days of 
starting prednisone, the patient began to notice a 
marked decrease of his stiffness (videotape segment 
2). He was able to decrease the dose of diazepam 
from 40 to 20 mg per day. A year later, his dose of 
prednisone has been decreased to 40 mg every other 
day, but he still requires 20 mg of diazepam daily for 
residual stiffness.
segments.evidence: Patient 2 CSF/serum GAD antibodies, other autoantibodies, HLA phenotype, and prednisone response are described.

segments.text:
Our two patients demonstrate the typical findings 
of SPS as described by Moersch and Woltman (1). 
Both fulfill the diagnostic criteria of Gordon et al. 
(2).
segments.evidence: The discussion states that both patients fulfilled SPS criteria and had typical findings.

EMG findings of continuous motor unit activity. 
The stiffness as well as the EMG findings improved 
after spinal anesthesia. 
In addition, both of our patients exhibited evi- 
dence of autoimmunity. Patient l had vitiligo and 
two sisters with IDDM; patient 2 had no recognized 
clinical autoimmune diseases, but had several se- 
rum autoantibodies and a sister with IDDM.
